title: Reflections on the journey to a Fair Pay Agreement so far

content.content: I am delighted to share that the Adult Social Care Negotiating Body for England Regulations 2026 were laid before Parliament on 3 November. This is a huge milestone for the adult social care sector and reflects two years of close collaboration and development with a wide range of colleagues and partners.

We are marking this milestone because these are the regulations that set out exactly how the government can and will run the Fair Pay Agreement process. The regulations establish the Adult Social Care Negotiating Body (ASCNB) and set the framework within which employer and worker representatives will negotiate a fair pay agreement for the adult social care workforce in England. They cover the Negotiating Body’s membership and appointments, governance, negotiation process, terms of reference and dispute resolution arrangements. The regulations do not themselves set pay, terms or conditions.

The regulations must be debated and approved by both Houses of Parliament before they come into effect. This is a significant step forward towards establishing the body ahead of the first negotiation cycle, which is planned to begin in April 2027.

This really has been a major undertaking, and we could not have reached this point without the support of the adult social care sector. Thank you to those who took the time to respond to the consultation and share their views with us, and to our partners, including trade unions, social care employers and local government, for working with us to shape the proposals.  We are deeply grateful.

The regulations still need to be debated in Parliament and secure approval, but laying the regulations means that we are now officially on track for the first negotiations to begin in April 2027 – leading to the first pay rise in workers’ pockets in April 2028.

title: Planning obligations at appeal – a complex picture

content.content: We've updated our procedural guidance after hearing that some of our wording caused confusion. Here's what changed and what our position is.

In April 2026, MHCLG brought in a regulation change which allows more appeals to follow the Part 1 route. This means that any appeal should be considered using the same evidence that the local planning authority (LPA) saw at application stage. A quicker decision is a welcome outcome, but the wider aim is to keep decision-making with the LPA wherever possible and avoid new material being introduced for the first time at appeal.
To make this a reality, and create the conditions for local, quicker decisions, behaviour change is required across the whole system.

Where there is proactive engagement between applicants and LPAs on planning obligations this may mean that fewer issues need to come to appeal, and at appeal there are fewer delays. That is why we keep looking at our procedures, and why we will continue to challenge ourselves and others to work towards agreed principles. We won’t always get it right first time, and we’re grateful to those who reach out in the appropriate way to tell us when we need to adapt.
Why we've updated the guidance

The Part 1 procedures for written representations appeals came into force on 1 April 2026. As they bedded in, we made some changes to our procedural guidance on planning obligations and on what an inspector takes into account.

These were intended as a minor clarification. Some of the wording went further than we meant, and people in the planning community told us it was being read as a change of approach. Thank you to those who raised it, including by commenting on our social media posts and meeting with us to talk it through.
What our position is
This is not a change to national planning policy. Procedural guidance explains how we run appeals.

It is good practice for a planning obligation to be submitted as part of the application when it is lodged with the local planning authority (LPA). For example, we see a number of appeals where a reason for refusal relates to a lack of obligation to secure necessary infrastructure. Having those discussions with the LPA as part of the application process could avoid that.

We appreciate that this may have resourcing implications. The government's wider work on national model obligations, referenced in the National Planning Policy Framework, could help with this in the future.

For written representations appeals, the expectation has always been that an executed and certified copy of any obligation is submitted when the appeal is made. Hearings and inquiries follow different deadlines.
What we've changed
Planning obligations
What the Inspector takes into account

We've restructured this section to make clear when we may consider new evidence after the LPA's decision. It applies where there has been a material change in circumstances, such as a change in policy, a relevant court judgement or a requirement for an Environmental Statement. It also covers cases where an executed planning obligation is needed and either:
How to stay up to date with future changes

You can sign up to email alerts when changes are made to GOV.UK pages. Look for the bell icon and sign up to 'get emails about this page'. This function allows anyone with an email account to receive an email when any change is made to that page.
Tell us what you think
If anything is still unclear, please speak to your case officer.
View the updated guidance
The guidance for appeals relating to applications dated on or before 31 March 2026 remains available on GOV.UK.

title: How your evidence can help protect our native seals and otters

content.content: English waters are home to many important and protected marine mammal species. Across our seas, inlets and coastal areas, we have two native seals species, grey seals (Halichoerus grypus) and harbour seals (Phoca vitulina), as well as one native otter species, the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra).

These species are protected within a type of marine protected area (MPA) known as a special area of conservation (SAC). Grey seals are protected within four SACs, while harbour seals are protected within one. There are two SACs on the coast which protect Eurasian otters. These MPAs help to protect important species, and they also protect the habitats that they rely on.
Seals

Seals rest in areas known as haulouts, often in colonies. Grey seals typically prefer exposed rocky coastlines, whereas harbour seals prefer more sheltered sandy beaches, tidal flats and estuarine zones. On land they can rest, warm-up, stay safe from predators, and look after their young, but they depend on the sea for food. Their diet is largely made up of fish and invertebrates which depend on healthy marine habitats. We know that grey seals eat a lot of sand eels, which live in sandy substrate habitats. This demonstrates why we need to consider the impacts of activities on habitats and how both are connected.
Otters

Otters shelter in dens known as holts. Holts are often found along shorelines with places to hide like ledges, rock piles, and dense scrub. They are generally solitary animals once a cub is no longer dependent on its mother.

Like seals, otters live on land but depend on the sea for food, often hunting in shallower waters according to the tide. Intertidal mudflats provide nursery areas for crustaceans which form a large part of coastal otter diets, so it is important that these habitats are protected.
Which activities may interact with seals and otters
Unfortunately, their life on the English coast means that these species are vulnerable to disturbance caused by human activities.

Our work considers the potential impact of marine Non-Licensable Activities (mNLA), which include a range of recreational and commercial activities, from anchoring, to boating, wildlife watching and kayaking.
Noise from motorised vessels caused by wildlife tour boats can travel through the air and underwater, which may disturb seals and otters in the surrounding area.

Even quieter activities may cause disturbance. Kayaks and canoes may alarm the animal if they “sneak up” on them. Although seals often show interest in divers and swimmers, it can be dangerous to both the humans and the seals if the seals are at risk of becoming distressed.
How seals and otters react to disturbance

Different levels of disturbance may result in different reactions from seals and otters. They may simply notice the disturbance, move away from it or even flee from land into the sea. Wherever they are disturbed, they will expend energy. Seals are particularly vulnerable to disturbance during pupping season. Grey seal pups are born with a white coat that is not waterproof so they cannot go into the sea when they are first born, so any disturbance could impact their chances of survival.
How activities may affect important habitats

Even if recreational activities are not directly impacting seals and otters, they can have other, knock-on effects. Anchoring on sensitive habitats such as reef, seagrass, and benthic seabed features can cause significant long-term damage. Thes habitats are integral to supporting the prey species that seals and otters need to survive. Therefore, it is vital we consider the whole environment when protecting species.
Have your say

We are currently seeking additional evidence on the impacts of mNLA on seals and otters, as well as other protected species and habitats. If you have relevant research, monitoring data, reports or observations, we ask you to respond to our current call for evidence and respond before it closes on 25 November 2026.
By sharing information, you can help improve our understanding of these impacts and support the effective protection of England’s seals, otters, and the supporting habitats.
For more detailed guidance on how to contribute, why this is important and the types of evidence that we find useful, please visit our previous blog:
Share your evidence on the impacts of recreational activities in England’s marine protected areas (MPAs) – Marine Development Blog
If you require support completing our survey or submitting evidence, please let us know: conservation@marinemanagement.org.uk

title: Building a long-term vision for tenant farming

content.content: Tenant farmers manage a third of all farmland in England. They are vital to food production, look after our land, support rural communities and underpin the £160 billion agri-food sector.

While it can be difficult to get into farming, the tenanted sector offers a route to new entrants that does not depend on owning land. Tenancies also provides a way for established farmers to expand and grow their farm businesses.
Defra Secretary of State Dame Angela Eagle spoke to the Tenant Farmers Association (TFA) National Executive Committee on 11 November and reaffirmed her commitment to supporting tenant farmers.

Dame Angela Eagle invited the tenanted sector to work with Defra to develop a shared plan to build a resilient, profitable and productive tenanted sector, as part of the government’s next step to deliver the Farming Roadmap.
Here is what was discussed and what it means for tenant farmers, landlords and advisers.
Developing a long-term vision
The Farming Roadmap and the Land Use Framework set out the government's vision for agriculture. They explain how we will use land to meet our food security and environmental goals over the long term.
Both recognise the importance of the tenanted sector in delivering these goals.
Partnership is key to achieving the vision that these strategies set out. We are starting to develop a long-term vision for tenant farming, in partnership with the sector, with two aims:

Over the coming months, we'll work with industry representatives - such as the TFA, CLA, NFU and professional bodies - to set up workshops with tenant farmers, landlords and advisors to gather views and ground our plan in lived experience.
Anyone interested in getting involved can contact Defra at agriculturaltenancies@defra.gov.uk and we will be in touch with a list of engagement opportunities in due course.
To achieve these outcomes, these workshops will help identify the barriers and issues facing the tenanted sector that need to be addressed. We want to see that:
Speaking on Defra's plan to develop a long-term vision for the tenanted sector, TFA Chief Executive George Dunn said:
Gavin Lane, Country Land and Business Association (CLA) President, said:
What we have done so far
This work builds on action we are already taking to support the tenanted sector:
Commissioner for the Tenant Farming Sector

We appointed Alan Laidlaw as England's first Commissioner for the Tenant Farming Sector and for over a year, Alan Laidlaw has been encouraging collaborative relationships between tenants, landlords and advisers.

Alan has provided a route for those who may feel unable to raise concerns themselves and has ensured that the voices of tenants across the country have been heard. The Commissioner’s office promotes awareness of the Agricultural Landlord and Tenant Code of Practice, highlights poor behaviours and systemic challenges, builds strong relationships across the sector, and feeds frontline insight into Defra policy development.

In year two, the Commissioner will expand engagement, strengthen intelligence-sharing, encourage greater sector ownership of the Code, and continue using evidence, case studies and reporting to support a thriving tenant farming sector.
You can read more about the work of the Commissioner in this blog post published last week.
If you want to raise an issue with the Commissioner’s office, you can contact them through the GOV.UK service or via email at ctfs@defra.gov.uk.
Farm Tenancy Forum

We’re reforming the Farm Tenancy Forum to give tenant farmers a bigger role in making policy. We understand that Tenant farmers may have different views depending on their type of tenancy, business and location.

We are therefore bringing together a Tenant Farmer Group so we can gather insights from a range of tenant farmers. The group will meet before each meeting of the Farm Tenancy Forum to discuss the issues the Forum will discuss. Two members will then go to the Forum and share the group's views, so they feed directly into policy.
Longer-term tenancies
Longer tenancies can help provide tenants the security needed to invest in food production and environmental improvements.
The Farm Tenancy Forum's guidance on longer-term tenancies sets out these benefits in more detail and provides clear guidance on what both landlords and tenants should consider.

Defra is working with larger and institutional landowners through the National Estate for Nature group to explore pioneering models of longer-term tenancies. These tenancy agreements have a specific focus on environmental improvement alongside food production.

By identifying and sharing best practice models that benefit both landlords and tenants and showing how they have been implemented in practice, we can encourage other landlords to take a similar approach.

title: Imagined bogs and future forests: maps for unlocking the potential of England’s landscapes

content.content: By Elizabeth Mitchell, senior officer for engagement and impact, and Chris Burstow, geospatial principal officer, both Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment programme

Where in England could nature do best, and how can we help wildlife move between habitats? Natural England's Habitat Network Maps, built on 27 priority habitats, suggest where to create new corridors, stepping stones and larger habitat patches. A major update has just been published, so we look back at why the maps were created, how they are already shaping Local Nature Recovery Strategies, nature-based solutions and private investment in Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG), and what has changed in the refresh.
The Habitat Network Maps
If we want to identify areas where nature could thrive in England, the Habitat Network Maps are a good place to start.

Based on existing maps of 27 priority habitats that underpin England's biodiversity, they suggest areas for expansion to help encourage habitat resilience – new corridors, stepping stones, or simply larger patch sizes.
And with a major update recently published, now feels like an excellent moment to look back at how the maps are shaping nature recovery planning across England.
Why did we create the Habitat Network Maps?

One vital strand in the maps’ origin story is the influential 2010 review led by Sir John Lawton, ‘Making Space for Nature’, which called for the most valuable habitats across the country to be 'better, bigger, more, and more joined-up'. It’s a report which is still widely cited, with its more detailed recommendations seeded through the Environment Act and the Environmental Improvement Plan, and embedded through much of Natural England’s operational activity. But to bring the report’s recommendations to life at a strategic, national scale we need large-scale, location-specific data – and this is where the Habitat Network Maps come in.

The first version of the maps was published by Natural England in 2020, while the work undertaken for this update was funded by the UK government under the Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment programme (NCEA).
What have the maps been used for so far?
The maps have been used in a variety of ways:
What’s new in this update?

As part of the recent update, the maps have been comprehensively refreshed using the latest datasets, including the Priority Habitats Inventory, Wood Pasture and Parkland Inventory, Agri-Environment Schemes data, Environment Agency flood zones, and Priority River Habitat headwater data.

Significant improvements to the mapping tool now offer greater flexibility, including allowing users to set custom geographic extents and select appropriate grid sizes. Grassland selection by soil type has also been enhanced.

Following consultation with Natural England habitat specialists, some individual habitat networks have been combined to better reflect current ecological understanding. Single networks – such as blanket bog, lowland meadows and ancient semi-natural woodland – remain distinct, while others now combine previously separate categories: coastal habitats, calcareous grasslands, heathlands, fen and reedbed habitats, and rivers and lakes.
These updates, informed by user feedback and scientific review, ensure the mapping is more accurate and practical for conservation planning.
The Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment programme

The Natural Capital and Ecosystem Assessment programme is assessing England's land, freshwater, and coastal ecosystems to produce a baseline of our natural assets by 2029, enabling a natural capital approach to policy and decision-making. As well as the Habitat Network Maps, it has provided vital support for several related mapping and data tools allowing us to better understand and manage our habitats, including the Priority Habitats Inventory, Ancient Woodland Inventory, and England Peat Map.

title: Victoria Barrow: developing procurement capability through a CIPS apprenticeship

content.content: Procurement and contracts officer Victoria Barrow feels much more confident and effective in her role after undertaking a Chartered Institute of Procurement and Supply (CIPS) apprenticeship.

Victoria joined Bishop Bewick Catholic Education Trust (BBCET) in October 2024 at a time when the organisation had undergone a period of significant growth. The Trust covers 39 schools across Newcastle, Northumberland and North Tyneside and had identified a need to strengthen its procurement capability as it grew.
Victoria brought extensive commercial experience from account management roles with major brands, but procurement was relatively new to her.
Building procurement capability

Recognising an opportunity to develop specialist knowledge internally, BBCET supported her enrolment on a CIPS Level 3 Procurement and Supply apprenticeship, fully funded by the employer apprenticeship levy.

“I didn’t have a background in procurement,” Victoria said. “The Trust asked whether I’d be interested in getting a qualification and I was really keen because it would help me understand procurement and supply from the ground up.”

The 18-month programme combines virtual learning, workplace projects, professional discussions and other assessments. Weekly online sessions, regular contact with a dedicated tutor and opportunities to apply learning directly to real projects have helped her balance the apprenticeship alongside a busy day job.

“It was a bit intimidating going back into education after many years,” said Victoria. “But the course was really well structured and the support from the tutors meant you couldn’t really fall off track.”
Real-world relevance from day one
One of the biggest benefits has been seeing her learning translate directly into workplace practice.

“As the months went on, everything started clicking into place,” she said. “The reason why we do things and why certain processes are in place. I think I'm performing better in my role because I've got that confidence and I've got that qualification behind me now.”

That growing confidence is already having an impact. Having completed her course and been awarded a Distinction, Victoria is now managing procurement projects with a greater degree of independence while also supporting wider Trust initiatives and contract management.

“My manager now can let me just run with projects,” she said. “There's one I've been working on for telephony and broadband. I've required very little support from my line manager with that, and she's got the confidence in me that I know what I'm doing with the process, and I can follow all the rules.”

Having internal procurement expertise also helps BBCET achieve better value for  money and reduce reliance on external support. Prior to Victoria doing the apprenticeship, much of the Trust’s procurement activity relied on costly external consultants.
According to Victoria, having qualified procurement knowledge within the organisation helps ensure projects are approached consistently, transparently and in line with procurement regulations.
Value of investing in people

“It's given me a lot more credibility in the workplace as well,” she said. “People in the trust know we've got a procurement professional and can start to see the value in procurement and doing it properly.”
Victoria believes the benefits extend beyond compliance, helping schools make better-informed purchasing decisions and maximise value from their budgets.
“Procurement isn’t always about choosing the cheapest option,” she said. “It’s about understanding the whole picture, considering value and making the right decision for the organisation.”

The experience has also reinforced the value of investing in the development of school business professionals, particularly at a time when schools and trusts are facing increasing financial pressures and operational complexity.
“I think it’s definitely worth investing in your people,” Victoria said. “You’re upskilling staff, giving them more confidence and credibility, and helping them feel more valued in their role.”

For BBCET, the investment is already delivering results by strengthening internal capability, reducing reliance on costly external expertise and developing the commercial and procurement skills needed to support a growing organisation.

The DfE has partnered with CIPS to strengthen procurement capability across schools and trusts. Through this partnership, schools and trusts can access training, resources and professional development opportunities, including CIPS apprenticeship programmes funded through the employer apprenticeship levy.

Any savings, benefits and outcomes described in this case study were provided by Bishop Bewick Catholic Education Trust and reflect its specific experience and circumstances. Individual results will vary between schools and trusts.

title: Women in hydrography: a Q&A on learning at sea through the IHO’s Empowering Women in Hydrography Project

content.content: In summer 2026, UK Hydrographic Office (UKHO) Senior Geospatial Specialist, Lizzie Davis, joined an international survey through the International Hydrographic Organization's (IHO) Empowering Women in Hydrography (EWH) Project.

Delivered in partnership with France's hydrographic and oceanographic service, SHOM, the programme brought together four women from different hydrographic organisations for a two-week deployment aboard the Research Vessel RV Pourquoi Pas? The EWH Project funded the participants so that they could join the vessel to learn from leading researchers and contribute to ongoing survey and oceanographic operations.
Fresh from returning to the UKHO, Lizzie shared her experience.
Getting there
How did you first hear about the opportunity?
I was looking for opportunities to gain more practical survey experience when I came across the Empowering Women in Hydrography initiative on the IHO website.

The programme immediately caught my attention because gaining hands-on survey experience was one of my professional development goals. I discussed the opportunity with my line manager, who was very supportive, and we agreed it would be a valuable way to build my skills while bringing additional experience back to the UKHO.

As part of the application process, I outlined how the placement would support my development and benefit my work. I also submitted information about my role and experience to the IHO, explaining why I wanted to take part in the programme.
What made you apply?

The opportunity appealed to me because it offered hands-on survey experience while giving me the chance to learn from other hydrographic organisations. I was interested in seeing how different teams operate, from the equipment they use to the procedures they follow.

I was also excited by the combination of hydrography and oceanography. While hydrography is my area of expertise, the placement offered an opportunity to develop my understanding of the wider science that supports survey work and gain experience in areas I would not normally encounter in my day-to-day role.
Life on board
What was a typical day like on board?

I worked mainly daytime hours, starting each day with a briefing on the vessel's planned operations and a review of the work completed overnight. The team also provided background on the scientific objectives behind each activity, helping us understand how our practical work contributed to the wider research programme.

Much of my time was spent supporting survey and oceanographic operations. This included assisting with the deployment of instruments which measure conductivity, temperature and pressure (CTDs) in the water column, and vertical microstructure profilers used to collect detailed oceanographic data.

The placement also provided an opportunity to work alongside scientists and observe data being collected and analysed in real time. Seeing how the survey and scientific teams worked together gave me a broader understanding of the research taking place and how different disciplines contribute to a successful survey campaign.
Was there a particular project or operation that stood out to you?

One of the highlights was working with a CTD rosette system. I have typically used a much smaller CTD instrument to collect sound velocity data for hydrographic surveys, but this system was equipped with a wide range of additional sensors to support multiple areas of research.

The CTD was deployed to depths of several thousand metres and collected measurements on everything from conductivity, temperature and pressure to ocean currents, light levels and chlorophyll. It could also collect water samples at different depths for further analysis.
What stood out most was seeing how much information could be gathered from a single deployment and how the data was used to build a detailed picture of the marine environment.
Seeing research in action
How did your hydrographic experience help during the survey?

My hydrographic experience allowed me to get involved in a range of activities throughout the two weeks. Having previously used CTD instruments during the UK Centre for Seabed Mapping’s joint survey back in May, I was already familiar with the equipment, the data it collects and how it can be used to support survey operations.

I also supported hydrographic data collection carried out by SHOM's team onboard to help identify suitable locations for scientific moorings to be positioned, ensuring monitoring equipment could be deployed safely and remain in place for long-term data collection.

The experience gave me valuable opportunities to contribute to discussions around survey planning and data collection. It was particularly interesting to see how hydrographic information and oceanographic research complemented each other, with different teams working together to support the scientific objectives.
How did working alongside both hydrographers and oceanographers broaden your understanding of the marine environment?

Much of the oceanographic research focused on internal waves and how they affect the propagation of sound through the water column. I found that particularly interesting because hydrographic surveys also rely on acoustic sensors to collect bathymetric data.

The experience gave me a greater appreciation of how ocean conditions can influence sound velocity and potentially affect the data collected during a survey. It highlighted the close relationship between hydrography and oceanography and helped me better understand the environmental factors that can influence the interpretation of survey data.
Learning from others
What made the experience such a valuable learning opportunity?

One of the highlights for me was the learning element built into the programme. Each afternoon, a researcher would give a presentation about their work, explaining the questions they were trying to answer and the data they were collecting. Because there were researchers from several organisations onboard, these sessions helped us understand the variety of research taking place on the vessel.

The presentations often sparked discussions between researchers, with people sharing ideas and offering feedback on each other's work. It created a collaborative atmosphere and was a great opportunity to learn about a wide range of scientific disciplines beyond my own area of expertise.
What was it like working alongside scientists and hydrographers from different countries? Did you notice any similarities or differences in the way organisations approach hydrography?

What surprised me most was how much we had in common. Although the participants came from Peru, Indonesia, Spain and the UK, we all work to the same IHO survey standards. That meant our approaches to data quality and validation were broadly aligned, even if our organisations deliver surveys in different ways.

The biggest differences were in how survey programmes are organised. It was fascinating to compare approaches and see how different organisations place emphasis on different parts of the process while still achieving the same high-quality outcome.
Women in hydrography
Why are initiatives like Empowering Women in Hydrography important?
One of the things I valued about the experience was that we all came from different backgrounds, career stages and organisations, but we were all on board to learn and develop our skills.

For some participants, the placement offered exposure to survey equipment and techniques that were not readily available in their own organisations. For others, it was an opportunity to broaden their knowledge, gain practical experience and learn from experts in a variety of disciplines.

The programme also created space to discuss our experiences as women working in hydrography and to learn more about the opportunities and challenges faced by colleagues in different countries. Bringing together people who are genuinely passionate about developing their skills and advancing the profession helps strengthen the global hydrographic community and supports the next generation of hydrographers.

For me, that was what made the experience so valuable. It provided an opportunity to gain practical survey experience purely for development, learn from experts in a range of disciplines and build connections with colleagues from around the world. I'd recommend it to anyone looking to broaden their skills and experience.

title: Developing AI policies that work for local government

content.content: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to help councils improve services and work more efficiently. To realise those benefits responsibly, councils need clear governance, which is usually set by an organisation's AI policy.

As part of the Local AI team's work to support safe and responsible AI adoption, we wanted to better understand how councils are developing and implementing AI policies. By identifying common challenges, gaps in available support, and examples of emerging practice, we can develop shared resources that provide a consistent baseline and avoid unnecessary duplication of effort.
What we did

The Responsible AI team within Local AI interviewed local government officials from over 15 councils who had been involved in developing AI policies within their organisations. The discussions explored how councils approached policy development, the impacts of those policies and the challenges they encountered along the way.

We heard from councils at very different stages of the journey. Some were developing their first policy, while others were already revisiting theirs, as technology, organisational understanding and the ways staff use AI evolved.

What came through strongly was an enthusiasm for sharing what had been learned. There were plenty of questions still being worked through, but also a real willingness to learn from each other and help others avoid having to start in the same place.
What we learned
Develop the policy with people across the council

AI policy is rarely the work of one team. Councils told us about bringing together colleagues from information governance, digital and IT, analytics, HR, finance, legal services, content design, trade unions and other parts of the organisation. That breadth matters. Different teams spot different risks and opportunities, and involving them early can help build wider understanding, ownership and support for the policy. Devon County Council, for example, set up an AI Steering Group and AI Board with representatives from across the organisation to oversee AI-related activity and consider its ethical implications.
Integrate AI policies into a wider governance system, so the policy doesn’t govern on its own

Councils we spoke to are supporting their policies with practical mechanisms that help staff know what they can use and what to do when a new opportunity arises. Denbighshire County Council, for example, has integrated its AI policy into its AI request process, helping ensure that people requesting access to AI tools are aware of the policy and its requirements. Another council we spoke to uses an AI Ethics Board to review proposed uses of AI across services. Another has introduced new technical controls to restrict access to unapproved AI services. These mechanisms turn written policies into operational decisions. Without them, staff may understand the policy but still be unsure what to do with it.
Don’t stop at just publishing the AI policy

Putting an AI policy on the intranet does not automatically mean people will know about it, understand it or know how it applies to their work. Councils we spoke to used combinations of staff bulletins, manager briefings, workshops, videos, dedicated AI pages, learning pathways and AI champions to bring their policies to life. Leeds City Council, for example, has incorporated AI into mandatory information governance training, developed a dedicated intranet area with guidance and training, and created an in-house 45-minute AI training course alongside further learning and supporting materials. Approaches like this help turn the policy from a static document into something that supports day-to-day decisions about responsible AI use.
Think about transparency from the start

Councils are also considering when and how residents should know that AI has contributed to a service, communication or decision. There is unlikely to be one answer for every use of AI. The level of transparency needed for a low-risk use may look very different from something that could significantly affect a resident. Councils are thinking about how people should be told about the use of AI in public services, what human oversight is in place, and what alternative routes to a service are available. Building these questions into the design of services is much easier than trying to add transparency after an AI tool has already been introduced.
Making AI policy easier to develop and use

Many councils have learned from their peers, adapting policies developed elsewhere and drawing on existing information management, data governance and other policies. While these are useful resources, a clear message from our interviews was the need for more practical support. Several officials said they would have found it helpful to have access to a template or framework covering the key issues an AI policy should address, while still allowing flexibility to reflect local governance structures, terminology and risk appetite.

Some councils also noted that existing guidance could be lengthy or difficult to navigate, making it harder to translate high-level principles into something practical. This suggests a need for resources that are both accessible and actionable, helping councils move from understanding responsible AI principles to implementing them.
This is where we hope our upcoming work can help.
What's next?
The findings of these interviews alongside broader engagement with local government stakeholders have been shaping the Responsible AI team's work to support councils adopting AI responsibly.
AI policy template

We are developing an AI policy template for councils, drawing on feedback from local authorities and a review of more than 40 council AI policies. It will provide a practical starting point for councils developing a policy for the first time, as well as those reviewing an existing one. The template helps councils ask the right questions, define responsibilities and support responsible adoption.
Responsible AI Charter

More immediately, the team is co-designing a Responsible AI Charter with councils. The Charter will set out a shared baseline of commitments for responsible AI adoption, providing something councils can build from while retaining the flexibility to decide how those commitments are put into practice locally.
We have already run several workshops to help co-design these products which have led to significant improvements. We are hoping to publish these resources by spring 2027.
If you'd like to be a co-design partner and help us shape the AI policy template for local government, please don't hesitate to get in touch with us by emailing LocalAI@communities.gov.uk.

To realise those benefits responsibly, councils need clear governance, usually set by an organisation's AI policy. Find out how the Local AI team is working with councils to develop shared resources that provide a consistent baseline and avoid unnecessary duplication of effort.

title: Remembering, recognising and supporting our Armed Forces community

content.content: In this week when we pause to remember and reflect on the service and sacrifice of those who have served our country, it is also an opportunity to recognise the Armed Forces community today. This includes veterans, and the spouses and partners who stand alongside them and provide invaluable support.

At GFiE, we are proud of the work we do to support veterans and their spouses and partners as they navigate the transition from military to civilian life. Leaving the Armed Forces is about much more than changing jobs. It can mean adapting to a different culture, finding a new sense of purpose, translating highly valuable skills and experience into civilian roles, and building new networks and connections.

That transition matters. Meaningful employment can play a vital role in helping people establish themselves in civilian society, bringing stability, confidence, opportunity and a renewed sense of belonging. Veterans and their families have so much to offer, and we believe that departments and agencies across the Civil Service benefit enormously from the skills, commitment, resilience and experience they bring.
During this week of remembrance, we honour those who served, recognise those who continue to serve, and reaffirm our commitment to supporting those who are building their next chapter.
Thank You

title: Understanding PFAS: what the Environment Agency's research reveals about “forever chemicals”

content.content: Few groups of chemicals have attracted as much attention in recent years as PFAS. At the Environment Agency, we're working to better understand where PFAS are found, how they move through the environment, and how their impact can be reduced. It's a complex challenge, but our growing evidence base is helping us build a clearer picture and show that action can make a difference.
What are PFAS and why do they matter?

PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are a large and diverse group of chemicals that have been used since the 1950s in many everyday items from textiles and food packaging to firefighting foams and industrial processes. They are resistant to heat, oil and water, making them valuable in a wide range of applications. The same chemical properties that make them very useful also have a downside; they break down extremely slowly, so once they are in the environment they remain there for a long time. This is why they are often called "forever chemicals".

Understanding PFAS is not straightforward. Thousands of different substances fall into this group, and scientists are still building a clearer picture of how they move through the environment and where they can be found. Some PFAS can accumulate in wildlife and people. Concerns about their persistence and potential impacts have led to increasing efforts globally to better understand where they occur and how risks can be managed. At the Environment Agency, we've been monitoring PFAS in England's waters for more than two decades and, over that time, our understanding of these substances has grown enormously.
How does the Environment Agency monitor PFAS?

One of the biggest challenges we face in managing risks from PFAS effectively is understanding the scale of the issue. We know these substances are used in a huge range of products and activities but understanding where they end up in the environment and how that changes over time requires a lot of knowledge.

That's why we published our updated assessment of PFAS sources, pathways and environmental data. Building on earlier work from 2021, the report draws on a much larger body of monitoring information to create a detailed picture of PFAS in English rivers, lakes, estuaries, coastal waters and sources such as landfill leachate. It also draws on new evidence from fish and other aquatic animals to improve our understanding of how PFAS can build up in wildlife.

The findings show just how much our understanding has developed. We now monitor more PFAS, across more locations, and with greater confidence than ever before. We found both positive signs of improvement and ongoing challenges.

Our report shows that concentrations of some long-regulated PFAS have fallen in English rivers and fish over recent years. While PFAS remain widespread in the environment, these findings show that regulatory action to reduce emissions can lead to real environmental improvements for certain PFAS in some parts of the water environment.

At the same time, better evidence is helping us understand the issue in greater detail. We are identifying new patterns, learning more about how PFAS move through different parts of the environment and improving our understanding of where future efforts may be needed.
Turning science into action

While PFAS are monitored in many water environments across England, relatively few established environmental standards or toxicology-based thresholds are available to help interpret environmental monitoring data for many of the substances we routinely detect. That can make it difficult to consistently assess monitoring results; further investigation may be needed to understand the significance of the concentrations measured.

To help address this, scientists in our Chief Scientist's Group recently developed threshold values for several commonly detected PFAS in surface waters. The work filled an important evidence gap by providing a scientifically robust way of interpreting monitoring data for substances where no equivalent thresholds were previously available. These thresholds are not regulatory limits, but they provide a more consistent way of understanding monitoring results and help identify where further investigation may be needed

Whilst we do not currently monitor PFAS in the air routinely, we published new research reviewing the latest evidence on airborne PFAS. This work explores how these substances are released to air, how they move through the atmosphere, and how they can be measured. Together, these projects build a clearer and more complete understanding of how PFAS behave in the environment, where risks may arise and how best to shape future regulatory action.
Working together

Managing PFAS requires collective action from across government, industry and the scientific community. The Environment Agency works closely with Defra, public health organisations, water companies, regulators, researchers and industry. We regulate activities that may release PFAS into the environment and building the evidence base helps us to better understand and reduce pollution at source.

This work contributes to wider efforts across government, including delivery of the Government's PFAS Plan, to improve understanding of PFAS and reduce their impacts on people and the environment. By strengthening the evidence base and sharing our findings openly, we can help ensure future decisions are informed by the best available science.
Find out more: PFAS reports and resources

You can learn more about our work on PFAS by exploring our latest research on PFAS sources, pathways and environmental data, as well as our recent work developing PFAS thresholds for water and air. We are also reviewing other chemical groups that may have similar properties to PFAS, such as fluoroaromatic compounds. For a broader overview of how government and regulators are working together on this issue, visit Defra’s PFAS action Plan. You can also read our previous work on PFAS incineration and water thresholds.

title: 🏠 Explainer: Major victory for 3 million leaseholders as government takes action on rip-off service charges

content.content: If you’re a leasehold homeowner, your rights and protections are about to get significantly stronger.
The government is on a mission to give millions of leaseholders greater control over their homes and the charges they pay for them.
Around 3 million leaseholders pay service charges in England, yet many do not know what sits behind them.
Paying to maintain, insure and repair your home is a normal part of homeownership. But for many flat owners, these decisions are made by someone else on their behalf.
That means costs can rise with little information about why or where the money is going. And challenging them can carry the real risk of footing your landlord’s legal bill - even if you win.
That is about to change.
From 1 April 2027, leaseholders will be able to:

🔎 See where their money goes: New legal rights will allow leaseholders to request more information about their service charges, including information going back further in time. Landlords will need stronger grounds to refuse to provide it.

💷 Challenge unfair costs more easily: You are no longer at risk of automatically footing your landlord’s legal bills for challenging something you think is unfair. The system will also be made fairer by giving leaseholders a new route to apply to recover their own legal costs in appropriate cases.
From 1 November 2027:
Less chasing and more information provided as standard.
Leaseholders will automatically get clearer information about:
Private landlords will also have to provide simpler, standardised service charge demands, financial accounts and annual reports.

Council and housing association leaseholders will benefit from the 1 November 2027 insurance and administration charge changes too. The simpler, standardised service charge demands, service charge accounts and annual reports will then extend to them from 1 November 2028.
💰 Could this help bring down my service charges?
It could help leaseholders push back on costs that are unreasonable, which is a major shift in power.

The new rights will give flat owners more of the evidence behind what they are being asked to pay, putting them in a stronger position to question costs that look wrong and challenge those they believe are unreasonable.
🔍 Landlords will also have to operate in a much more transparent and accountable way.

Clearer information, accounts and service charge demands will make it harder for poorly explained costs to go unchallenged, while fairer rules on legal costs will make it less risky for leaseholders to take action where they believe charges are unreasonable.
That means greater pressure on landlords to justify how leaseholders’ money is being spent and to manage those costs properly from the outset.

The reforms do not cap service charges because buildings still need to be maintained, repaired and insured. But where costs are unreasonable, leaseholders will have more information, stronger protections and a fairer route to challenge them.
🤔 Wait, what actually is a service charge?
If you own a flat, you’ll usually pay towards the costs of looking after the building and the spaces you share with your neighbours, such as:
The difference from owning a house, which is usually freehold, is that someone else often manages these things on your behalf - so you’re paying towards costs you don’t necessarily control yourself.
That’s why homeowners should be able to see what they’re paying for and why and have a fair opportunity to challenge costs they believe are unreasonable.
➡️ And there’s more reform to come
These new protections are part of a much wider shake-up of leasehold.

The Prime Minister has pledged to introduce the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill in Parliament before Christmas, bringing further reforms to give existing and future flat owners greater rights, protections and control.
The Bill will include the already announced plans to:
🏠 Commonhold means owning the freehold of your flat and having a greater say with other owners over how your building is run.

title: Keeping Pace

content.content: Would £10 solve your financial challenge this Christmas? Would an extra 25p a week take the pressure off your cost of living? Do you think you could find somewhere to rent if rents keep going up but your rent allowance has been frozen for three years?

Most social security benefits are uprated fairly regularly. But some aren’t. Some rates of benefit have been frozen since they were introduced in the 1970s. Some are occasionally uprated, but often frozen.

For the last six months we in the Social Security Advisory Committee have been looking at the benefit rates, thresholds and caps which don’t form part of the regular social security uprating process We wanted to find out how many there are, and what effects the freezes are having, and recommend to the Government a sensible, less arbitrary, way of approaching them.

In some ways, this is a personal journey. I’m coming to the end of my ten years on the Committee. But much of my career before then had been working as a civil servant on social security policy and operational design in the Department for Work and Pensions and its predecessors. I was a very junior member of the team which introduced Income Support and Housing Benefit with an earnings disregard (the amount you could earn each week without losing benefit) at £5 for a single person. In the 1990s I led the team which designed Jobseeker’s Allowance - which inherited the £5 disregard from Income Support. Ten years later I helped implement Pension Credit which incorporated an earnings disregard of - wait for it - £5. I’ve now been retired for 13 years and the single person’s disregard in Housing Benefit,[1] Jobseeker’s Allowance and Pension Credit is still £5. It had a purpose when it was introduced in the 1980s – to allow people to earn a modest amount of money without it affecting their benefit or having to report it. Now that it’s worth 24 minutes’ work at the National Living Wage it is very hard to see what real purpose it has today.

This is only one example. Our overall conclusion is that what governments are doing when they freeze benefits like this is not just letting inflation decide the value of benefits, they’re also letting inflation change the purpose of benefit rules and sometimes the numbers and types of people affected too.

So what should the government do? We’re not saying they should just return all rates, thresholds caps to their original values, and maintain them there. Governments must have the freedom to decide on affordability and priorities.
But we are saying that:

If you want to learn more about our detailed findings and recommendations you can find our report here: SSAC Occasional Paper 28: Keeping Pace? Reviewing benefits, thresholds and caps in a changing economy - GOV.UK
[1] Although it now applies to pensioners only.

title: From carbon stores to carbon opportunities: a new map for nature recovery

content.content: Author: Sonja Schmidt, PhD, Natural England Senior Specialist – Climate Change

England's habitats and soils hold vast amounts of carbon, but some places store far more than others, and some have lost much of what they once held. A new Natural England StoryMap and mapping tool brings together carbon storage, sequestration and loss in one place, so you can see where protecting or restoring land could do the most good for climate and nature. Find out why peat soils matter so much, why the answer isn't always more trees, and how planners, land managers and local authorities can put the evidence to work.
A new Natural England StoryMap and mapping tool shows where protecting and restoring habitats could store the most carbon.
As world leaders meet at COP31, the UN's annual climate conference, one of our most powerful allies in tackling climate change is right beneath our feet.

England's habitats and soils hold huge amounts of carbon. Woodlands, grasslands, wetlands and peatlands all lock it away, but not equally. Some places store far more than others, some are capturing more carbon year after year, and some have lost much of what they once held.
For anyone planning nature recovery, that raises a practical question: with limited time and money, where will action make the biggest difference?
A new way to see the picture

Natural England has launched the Spatial Prioritisation of Land Management for Carbon StoryMap  and mapping tool to help answer that question. A StoryMap is an interactive web page that combines maps, text and images to walk you through the evidence.
The tool brings together three things that have not previously been easy to see side by side:
Seen together, they show where protecting what we already have, or restoring what has been lost, could do the most good for both nature and climate
Not all land is equal
Peat soils are carbon heavyweights. Some of England’s largest below-ground carbon stores are found in peat-rich landscapes, making protection of existing peat carbon a major priority.

Drained lowland peat is a major carbon-loss hotspot. Drainage and intensive cultivation expose carbon-rich peat to oxidation and continuing greenhouse-gas emissions. Areas such as the Fens therefore represent important opportunities for better water and land management.

The answer isn’t always more trees. Woodland creation can deliver substantial carbon gains on suitable mineral soils, but planting on carbon-rich peat can put much larger soil carbon stores at risk. It is about putting the right habitat in the right place.

Carbon storage and sequestration vary greatly between habitats and locations, so targeting matters. Restoring the right places can deliver much greater climate benefits, while also supporting wildlife, healthier soils and more resilient landscapes.
From map to action
The tool is designed to support the people making decisions about the land.

For instance, a team drawing up a Local Nature Recovery Strategy can use it to identify the areas where restoration would add the most carbon benefit alongside other priorities. Local authorities and environmental partnerships can use it to align climate action with nature recovery at a landscape scale. Land managers and conservation practitioners can use it to understand how carbon is distributed across the places they work.
It is a guide for landscape-scale planning. For decisions about individual sites, it should be used alongside local evidence and expertise.
Helping England reach net zero

Healthy habitats cannot replace the need to cut emissions, but they have an important role to play. By showing where nature recovery can deliver the greatest carbon benefits, this evidence can help target that supports England's net zero ambitions as well as wildlife recovery.
Explore the tool
The StoryMap introduces the datasets, evidence and methodology behind the tool, and lets you explore the maps yourself.
If you want to go further, you can access the underlying open datasets through the Natural England Open Data Geoportal, and find supporting evidence through the Access to Evidence catalogue.

title: When fire devasted our school, the RPA was there
authors: Mungo Sheppard, Headteacher, Ash Green Community Primary School

content.content: On 1 February 2022, an arson attack destroyed the entire key stage 2 block at Ash Green Community Primary School in Calderdale.

Mungo Sheppard, headteacher at Ash Green Community Primary School talks about how being a member of the Department for Education’s (DfE’s) Risk Protection Arrangement (RPA) – the department’s alternative to commercial insurance, supported his school to rebuild after this devastating arson attack.

That night we were incredibly fortunate that fire crews arrived quickly, managing to save the rest of the school. Our fire doors also played a crucial role in containing the blaze. Even so, a large part of the building was gone. The rest had smoke and water damage.

Our school is a member of the DfE’s Risk Protection Arrangement (RPA), calling them was top of my list that night. Their support was immediate. Together with our local authority, they guided us through a salvage operation that started straight away. That meant partial demolition and temporary repairs so we could keep going.

I cannot overstate how much that mattered. I did not have to work out what to do alone while dealing with a crisis. Today, we are fully rebuilt, with all our children back on the original site, but it has been quite a journey.
Building a village of cabins

It was a strange process, starting with quite literally fighting fires. The initial phase was all about addressing operational and strategic needs with the long-term goal of rebuilding bigger and better.

In the aftermath of the fire, we were fortunate to have an incredible team working with us, including colleagues from the RPA and strategic leaders managing the project. We moved about a third of the pupils to our lower site and some to other sites in the community that had opened up to us. We provided learning and food packs to the remaining children.

The first few weeks were intense, balancing the care of our children with the massive task of clearing the site and auditing everything lost in the fire. Teams worked tirelessly, taking down ceilings, removing floors, and addressing water damage. Every computer was meticulously cleaned and tested. Security was maintained 24/7, and demolition companies began removing dangerous structures.

Other local schools offered us places and we were grateful, but our community wanted to stay together. By the end of February half term, all children were back on our upper site, in cramped but workable rooms.

The next phase involved setting up portable cabins and within three weeks, we had a new kind of village with classrooms, intervention spaces, and all necessary facilities. The children and volunteers from the community all helped move the new resources to start working in those portable cabins.

It felt like running two roads at once. One was keeping school going day to day, the other was a huge building project. Weekly meetings with architects, the Department for Education and the local authority kept both moving.

As we moved into 2023, the demolition of the old building left a huge void where the school used to be. Seasonal changes brought new challenges, like setting up scaffolding corridors to protect children from harsh weather.
By summer 2023, we had put the project out to tender, we were determined to provide the best possible environment for our children.

The children had a front-row seat. From their cabins, they watched their new school rise. We took them to see the foundations when it was safe. We also ran virtual tours for pupils and families. The excitement grew with every update.
The difference it made

We were all thrilled as the project progressed, and with the support of the RPA. In July 2024, we held an opening ceremony. Seeing the children's faces on their first day in the new classrooms was priceless.

Now we have this incredible building, the first net zero building in Calderdale, which is doing so much good for our environment. It’s the smartest, newest school building in the area, and it’s been an amazing piece of work. Talking about it makes me feel humble but immensely proud.
Our new extension fits in with the old Victorian building. It has extra solar panels and is the first net zero building in Calderdale. We even gained more playground space.

The whole journey took 30 months. It felt like the longest 2 and a half years of my career. But it brought our community closer together in amazing ways. Our children are in this incredible building, giving us a brighter future.
You can hear more about Mungo's experience of being an RPA member when he joins the RPA Power Hour webinar on 19 November at 2pm.
Register to join the Power Hour.

Has your school or trust joined the Risk Protection Arrangement yet? The RPA is open to state-funded schools and academy trusts across England. Joining gives you cover and support to help you recover if the worst happens as well as other benefits. Find out more and join on GOV.UK.

Any savings, benefits and outcomes described in this blog were provided by Ash Green Community Primary School and reflect its specific experience and circumstances. Individual results will vary between schools and trusts.

title: Designing an AI assistant people can trust

content.content: The problem we set out to solve

When someone at Defra has an idea for how to use artificial intelligence (AI), how do they know if AI is suitable, and who can help? We built two connected features in the Defra AI digital toolkit. The first, “Check if AI is right for your idea”, helps people assess their ideas. The second, 'Ask the Toolkit', answers questions using the toolkit’s own guidance.
Here, I’ll explain how we designed the Ask assistant to help people find guidance, check answers and get support when they need it.
See Ask the Toolkit in action

Here’s how it works in practice. We asked, “How do I decide whether AI is the right approach for my service?” The answer suggests checking whether a simpler option, such as a search, a formula or a script, would do the job better. It also explains how the AI Capability and Enablement team scores requests.

We then asked a follow-up: “Can you give me an example of a good and a bad use case?” The assistant understood we were still talking about AI suitability. It gave examples from the toolkit’s pilots, such as checking expenses claims against policy. It also explained what makes a poor fit: tasks with one right answer every time, or where the data is hard to reach.

Each answer ends with “Guidance used” links to the toolkit pages it drew on, so people can check the source. It also reminds them that AI can make mistakes and offers a way to report a problem or get help from a person.
Check the answer against the source

Our guiding principle was that giving a wrong answer about a rule is the failure that matters most. An AI language model can sound confident while explaining a policy incorrectly. So, we check its answer before showing it to the user.

We run two checks first. We remove any source link that does not point to a page provided by our service. We also check quoted rules against the source page. A quotation only appears if its exact words are on that page. If the model has used different words, we remove the quotation and show a plain explanation with a link instead.
Sometimes that means a less impressive answer, and that’s deliberate. We would rather show less information than present a rewritten explanation as the policy’s own wording.
Designing for when things go wrong

We designed the difficult cases first, because that’s where trust is won or lost. The assistant has a separate heading and message for each outcome: answered, needs more detail, cannot answer, talk to a person, blocked and error.
Wording mattered more than we expected. When a question is blocked, we avoid words like “flagged” or “filtered”. These can sound like an accusation to someone unfamiliar with the technology.

Feedback from people who tested the service helped us improve the wording. “The toolkit does not cover this yet” left people stuck. The message now encourages them to contact the AI Capability and Enablement team.
We also changed what happens when an answer fails. The user sees an error message at the top of the page, and their question stays in the box. We do not add the failed answer to the conversation.
Small details that carry weight
Several changes I'm proudest of are tiny:
Running tests before the AI model was ready

We built the Ask feature with prepared answers before the AI model was ready. A setting let us switch these on for quality assurance, and the service matched keywords in questions to those answers. This let us review the wording, check accessibility and run through every outcome before connecting a working AI model.
Assistant, not autopilot

I see AI as an assistant, not an autopilot. It can help you find information and spend less time searching, but it does not replace professional judgement. Check the source, consider the context and remain responsible for how you use the answer.

Ask the Toolkit is one of Defra’s first public-facing AI tools. We have deliberately started with a clearly defined use case so we can test it carefully, learn from how people use it and strengthen security before applying what works elsewhere.
Making the service public also lets us show our approach to AI in practice: begin with a real need, use trusted guidance, test carefully and keep people accountable for the outcome.
More information
Farhana Abdul Alim is a Software Developer in the AI Capability and Enablement team.
Farhana plans to write a follow-up blog, where she will explore how she built the Ask assistant and considered different ways for users to prove their identity.

title: Asset management funding to help councils strengthen their cyber resilience

content.content: Strengthen your council's cyber resilience with £50,000 of funding and specialist support to improve your asset management and cyber resilience.

Local Digital is launching a new asset management support offer to help English councils and mayoral strategic authorities improve their asset management capabilities and strengthen their cyber resilience.

Through the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF) for local government, we have identified maintaining an accurate view of the technology systems, devices, software and digital services operating across their council as a common challenge.

Effective asset management is foundational to wider cyber security and resilience. Without effective asset management, councils may be unable to secure, maintain or recover critical assets, increasing their exposure to cyber threats.
To help address this challenge, Local Digital is launching a new asset management support offer for councils and mayoral strategic authorities.

The asset management support offer forms part of Local Digital's wider support for councils. We are launching it alongside a second round of CAF support funding, which will allocate up to £7 million in grants for up to 50 councils that have completed their CAF assessment, helping them accelerate improvements to their cyber resilience.
About the asset management support
The support is designed to help councils strengthen and accelerate their asset management capability, reducing their cyber risk.
The programme will provide a combination of funding and specialist support to help councils:
Successful councils will receive:
Councils will receive support tailored to their starting point and current asset management capability.
The funding can support councils to increase their asset management capability by helping them to:

Councils will be expected to make significant progress over the next 12 months, aligned with the Indicators of Good Practice (IGP) in the CAF for local government. Depending on their starting point, councils will be expected to work towards meeting the IGPs for asset management.

We also welcome applications from councils that consider themselves to have already met the IGPs for asset management. Strong asset management provides a foundation for wider cyber resilience. This support can help councils build on that foundation and drive further improvements in areas such as vulnerability management and supply chain security.
