title: Woodland carbon and productive forestry: how the Woodland Carbon Code works in practice

content.content: The Woodland Carbon Code has been part of the UK’s land use landscape for 15 years. I have been involved in its development and governance since it was introduced, nearly 20 years ago.

It was created to help bring private finance into woodland creation, while maintaining the high standards expected of a high quality carbon scheme. At the time of its introduction, the domestic woodland carbon market could have been described as the 'wild west', and was suffering serious criticism in the media.

Interest in carbon markets and domestic timber is growing. Along with that interest come questions about what kind of woodland the code supports, particularly whether it supports productive and commercial forestry. These are fair questions. Woodland creation involves long-term investment, a mix of public grants and private finance, and a regulatory framework designed to protect environmental standards.
What is additionality and why does it matter?

At the heart of the code is a principle called additionality. This means that carbon units must represent a genuine reduction in atmospheric carbon dioxide, one that would not have happened without carbon finance.
The code applies 2 tests:

For commercial forestry, financial additionality is often the most important consideration. If a productive woodland would be viable through timber income and public grants alone, then issuing carbon units for it would undermine the credibility of the carbon credit and the scheme itself.

This discipline is precisely why the code has become a respected and robust scheme. It’s the first government‑run carbon standard to reach the full assessment process of the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market, a body that assesses the quality of carbon credit schemes worldwide. Weakening the financial additionality test would put this credibility, and the code’s support for productive forestry, at risk. Some within the commercial forestry sector feel that it is 'stacked' against them. The grant figures later show why that’s not the case, and what it takes to pass it.
Productive forestry in context

People often assume that commercial plantations dominate England’s woodland. In reality, they don’t. Conifers currently make up around 23% of England’s woodland area, down from about 28% in 2010.1 This is reflected in the 50‑year softwood availability forecast, meaning the UK may have less home-grown softwood in future, at a time when global demand for timber is expected to rise sharply.
Since 2000, England has created 85,690 hectares of new woodland. Of that, only 6,140 hectares is conifer.2 That gap is often overlooked.

Given this, supporting a domestic supply of both timber and carbon is strategically important. The real challenge is not whether we should support productive forestry but how to make sure carbon finance goes only to projects that genuinely need it.
Grants and financial additionality
The way woodland creation grants and carbon finance interact is often misunderstood, especially for productive or conifer‑dominated schemes.

Woodland creation grants are more generous in England than in Scotland and Wales, reflecting England’s economic situation and the value of land. For example, the England Woodland Creation Offer provides:

On poorer land, and with fast‑growing species such as Sitka spruce, it can be difficult to show that the woodland wouldn’t be planted without carbon finance. Because of this, the code limits how much grant a project can claim. This is based on a transparent cashflow assessment that considers:
This transparent process also means third-party validators can scrutinise projects without having to pick through endless financial models and statements.

A project can always pass the financial additionality test; where the level of grant support would otherwise prevent a project from passing the financial additionality test, accepting a lower grant will enable it to pass. The appropriate combination of public funding, carbon finance and private investment will depend on the economics of the individual project. This makes sure carbon finance goes where it makes a real difference, without replacing investment that would have happened anyway.
Illustrative grant outcomes by woodland type

The table below shows how much grant a 100‑hectare woodland creation project in England could claim, per hectare, depending on land quality and species mix, while still passing the financial additionality test. These figures assume mid-range establishment costs.
*Good land quality is defined as Agricultural Land Classification grades 1, 2 and 3; poor is defined as grades 4 and 5.

These figures make an important point: productive woodland is supported, but grant levels and carbon finance must reflect its underlying economics. Designing a scheme to maximise short‑term grant income won’t always give you the best long‑term woodland value or timber returns.

Sitka spruce, as the mainstay of the commercial timber sector, generally grows faster and has a shorter rotation than other conifers, so it’s treated differently in the financial additionality test. Even in a woodland managed for timber, adding a wider mix of species can significantly affect the level of grant you can claim, while still passing the test. Diversifying the species mix will also make the woodland more resilient to the effects of climate change and to pest and diseases.
Getting consent and funding without delay

Creating a new woodland in the UK is regulated to meet Environmental Impact Assessment regulations and the requirements of the UK Forestry Standard. The Forestry Commission bases consent decisions on evidence, not simply on the number of objections received. We’ve published maps showing areas with no known sensitivities for woodland creation, which can help you choose planting sites where getting consent should be more straightforward.

You can get funding through the Woodland Creation Planning Grant to help develop compliant well‑designed proposals. Where a site is straightforward and planting stock has been ordered, planting within a year of application is achievable.
The key to a fast decision is choosing a site without sensitivities and preparing a plan with all the necessary information from the start. To support this, the Forestry Commission has introduced:
How long does woodland carbon last?
A common concern among investors is how durable woodland carbon really is.

Woodland is a permanent land use in the UK, as set out in the 1967 Forestry Act and 1998 Environmental Impact (Forestry) Regulations. Tree carbon stocks change through thinning, harvesting and restocking, but the land itself stays as woodland. To reflect this, the code limits the number of woodland carbon units it issues, based on how the woodland is managed, so units reflect the long-term increase in carbon stocks, averaged over several management cycles, rather than the highest carbon stock at maturity.

The code also manages risk through a pooled buffer. 20% of all woodland carbon units issued go into this buffer and are never sold. It covers the small number of permanent losses caused by development or severe natural disturbance. On top of this, the number of units a project can claim is reduced by a further 20% at the planning stage to prevent projects overestimating their carbon savings.

Recent analysis looked at current rates of permanent woodland loss from development and natural disturbance. It found that woodland carbon under the code lasts for an estimated 2,300 years. This makes it one of the most durable, nature‑based, carbon options available.
The Woodland Carbon Code and harvested wood products

Of course, when trees are harvested, much of the carbon remains as ‘harvested wood products’ in some cases for many decades or even centuries, representing another pool of durable carbon. However, the code only accounts for carbon within the forest boundary, where it can be measured and independently verified. The UK’s national greenhouse gas inventory does include harvested wood products, but the code operates at a project scale.

Currently, it is not possible to track individual timber batches through mills, into finished products, and through their working life, without risking double counting. If woodland owners could claim carbon in harvested wood products, the businesses using that timber further down the supply chain couldn’t also claim a carbon credit for using low-carbon materials. This would undermine their own low-carbon claims.

However, Grown in Britain has published the Biogenic Stored Carbon Quotient, the UK’s first certification scheme to measure and verify how much carbon is stored long-term in buildings using timber and other biogenic materials.
For now, keeping the boundary at the forest gate is essential for maintaining confidence in the carbon units issued and the reputation of the code.
Looking ahead

The code supports native, mixed and productive woodland, as long as carbon finance and public funding are applied proportionately and reported transparently. Its strength lies in its consistency, credibility and conservative design. Maintaining these safeguards will also be essential as government explores new ways of giving woodland creators greater certainty over future carbon revenues, while attracting more private investment into woodland creation.

As the UK looks to scale up woodland creation and attract private finance, the challenge isn’t choosing between carbon, timber or nature. It’s about aligning all three in a way that maintains trust and long‑term value.
For landowners and investors, well‑designed woodland remains a resilient, long‑term asset, delivering carbon, timber and wider public benefits within a robust and trusted framework.
Having worked on the code from the start, I’m confident that maintaining its credibility is what will support confidence for investors into the future.

description: Mark Broadmeadow, Head of Climate Change at the Forestry Commission, explains how the Woodland Carbon Code works, why certain safeguards exist, how productive and commercial forestry fit within the scheme and addresses some common misconceptions.

title: How should schools prepare for snow, storms and flooding, and will they close?

content.content: Schools and other education settings should stay open during severe weather wherever it is safe and reasonably possible. With effective planning, most settings can adapt and keep operating safely in storms, flooding, snow, ice, high winds, heatwaves and extreme cold.

Schools are responsible for their own plans and policies on how to deal with severe weather conditions. These plans help schools operate safely and reduce disruption. Before winter, schools should check that their business continuity and emergency plans are up to date and cover severe weather risks.
How can schools adapt to snow, ice and storms?
Adaptations will vary depending on the type of weather and local conditions, but schools may consider measures such as:
Should schools stay open in bad weather?

Yes. Schools should remain open with normal attendance, except in rare circumstances where it is unsafe to do so. Being in school helps pupils learn and reach their potential and supports working parents – and children may not be any safer outside of school in severe weather. Planning and practical changes can usually help schools manage severe weather safely.

School leaders should close a school or reduce attendance only as a last resort, following a careful local risk assessment. Other local schools closing does not necessarily mean your school needs to close. If attendance must be restricted, schools should prioritise vulnerable children, children of critical workers and children taking exams. Schools should also provide remote education for pupils who cannot attend and tell parents promptly.
When should schools close in severe weather?
School leaders should use a local risk assessment to decide whether they can stay open safely. They should consider the following factors, alongside any other local risks:
Schools should not assume that disruption to transport or difficulty travelling for some staff or pupils makes full closure unavoidable.
Which weather warnings should schools monitor?

Schools should monitor guidance from relevant bodies such as the Met Office and, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) and Environment Agency. This includes weather warnings and alerts covering storms, flooding, snow, ice and extreme wind.
UKHSA Weather-Health Email alerts provide early warning when adverse temperatures are likely to impact health and wellbeing
Environment Agency Flood Warnings will warn you about risk of flooding from rivers, the sea, or groundwater, by text, phone or email.
A weather warning or alert does not automatically mean a school should close. Alerts help schools understand the risks and decide what extra action may be needed.
What to do if your school closes

If a school does decide to temporarily close, it should keep the period of disruption as short as possible and reopen as soon as it can safely do so. It should consider moving to remote learning for pupils  until it is safe to reopen. This may include online lessons, recorded teaching, learning resources or independent work to complete at home.
There is specific guidance schools should follow if exams or assessments may be disrupted.
Tell parents as early as possible what remote education will be provided, how pupils can access it and what support is available.
Schools should not take an afternoon register and then offer large-scale 'optional' early collection of pupils immediately afterwards.
How should schools inform parents?

Schools should communicate clearly with parents ahead of periods of severe weather. Communications should make clear that the school will remain open wherever it is safe to do so and that pupils are expected to attend as normal unless parents are informed otherwise.

If normal arrangements need to change, tell parents as early as possible. Explain why the changes are needed and what the school is doing to stay safe. Include any changes to entrances or exits, transport, uniform, outdoor activities or other parts of the school day. Tell parents when they will receive the next update.
If a decision is taken to restrict attendance or close the setting, schools should communicate that decision promptly and explain the rationale for it.
How can settings support clinically vulnerable children during cold weather?

Settings should plan for children’s individual needs when assessing cold-weather risks, taking account of advice from parents, carers or clinical teams. Younger children and those with underlying or complex health conditions may be more vulnerable to the effects of cold weather. The UK Health Security Agency and Department for Education have produced specific guidance for education professionals on this.
How should settings manage seasonal illness in the colder months?
Some illnesses circulate more in autumn and winter. Read our blog on reducing the spread of illness this winter for seven practical steps that settings can take to keep pupils and staff healthy.

title: Unused bass authorisations: applications open
authors: Fisheries Management Team, Marine Management Organisation

content.content: The Marine Management Organisation (MMO) has opened applications for new sea bass fishing opportunities.

This follows recommendations from our 2025 review of bass authorisations. The review was an action set out under goal 2 of the bass fisheries management plan (FMP), which aims to balance fair access to the bass fishery with the long-term sustainability of bass stocks.
As a result, we're making 65 unused bass authorisations available through a new application process.
Why we're opening applications
Since 2015, sea bass (Dicentrarchus labrax) has been carefully managed to help the stock recover.

Measures such as catch limits, seasonal closures and authorisations have helped reduce fishing pressure on bass stocks. To commercially catch and retain bass using certain fishing gears, fishermen must hold a bass authorisation. You can find more information in our Bass Fishing Guidance.

The review found that over the years, the number of vessels with bass authorisations has reduced. It also highlighted the importance of supporting coastal fishing businesses and communities where possible.

Making these unused authorisations available means more eligible fishermen may have the opportunity to enter the bass fishery, while maintaining existing management measures that support the long-term sustainability of the stock.
If you already hold a bass authorisation, this process will not affect your existing access.
Who can apply
Applications are open for English licensed commercial fishing vessels administered by MMO to apply for an authorisation to land bass caught using hooks and lines gear.
Applications only apply to vessels 8-metre-and-under with a single hull (monohull) that do not currently hold a bass authorisation.
How the application process works
Applications open today, Monday 9 November 2026 and close on Monday 21 December 2026, giving applicants six weeks to apply.

If your application meets the eligibility criteria, we will enter it into a ballot. Successful applicants will then be offered a bass authorisation with certain restrictions, which will be listed in the guidance document.
Find guidance explaining how to apply and what information you'll need to provide on the MMO Fisheries Management Plan Updates page on GOV.UK.
Help and support
We know applying for a new fishing opportunity can raise questions.
That's why MMO teams will be visiting ports and coastal locations to talk through the process, answer questions and support anyone who would like help with their application.
Details of these visits will be published on the FMP events page.
If you have any queries, please contact us at bassapplications@marinemanagement.org.uk
Keep up to date
You will find the latest information about the application process on the MMO Fisheries Management Plan Updates page on GOV.UK.

description: Following MMO's review, unused bass authorisations are available to eligible commercial fishing vessels. Find out who can apply and how the process works.
